The hinge 16 may be a pin hinge, a pair of interleaved knuckles on a common pin, or a flexible hinge section integral with the frame, provided that it holds the frame halves in register when they are closed. Closure of the frame halves in register is relied upon by the cam drive described below, so the hinge 16 and the releasable latch 18 are arranged to bring the two frame halves to a repeatable closed position rather than merely to hold them near one another.

A plurality of jaw carriages 22 is distributed circumferentially about the closed frame. In the form shown in FIG. 1 the plurality of jaw carriages 22 consists of three jaw carriages 22 distributed about the closed frame. Three carriages define a stable seat on a round pipe without over constraining it. The synchronizing relationship described below is not limited to that number, and a clamp having more than three jaw carriages 22 is built in the same way, each additional jaw carriage 22 being coupled to the cam ring by its own follower and its own oblique slot as described below.

The frame carries a mounting boss 66, which stands radially outside the cam drive described below. The mounting boss 66 supports a sensor, a tool or a conduit on the split pipe clamp 10 and may be a threaded pad, a dovetail, a flange with fastener holes, or any other fitting suitable for the item to be carried. The mounting boss 66 does not participate in advancing or synchronizing the jaw carriages 22. A load applied to the mounting boss 66 is therefore reacted through the frame and into the jaw pads, and is not carried by the cam drive, so a moment applied by a carried instrument does not disturb the setting of the jaws.

Jaw carriages and jaw pads

Referring to FIG. 2, each jaw carriage 22 is slidable in a respective radial guide 24 of the frame. The radial guide 24 may be a rectangular slideway, a pair of parallel rails, or a bore that receives a cylindrical shank of the jaw carriage 22, and it constrains the jaw carriage 22 to travel along a radial path toward and away from the central axis of the closed frame. Two of the radial guides 24 are formed in one of the frame halves and the remaining radial guide 24 is formed in the other frame half in the illustrated form, so that each frame half carries at least one jaw carriage 22 and each frame half is loaded by the clamping action.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a jaw pad 26 that is mounted on the jaw carriage 22 for pivoting movement about a pad axis and that presents a concave bearing surface toward the central axis of the closed frame. Because the jaw pad 26 pivots relative to the jaw carriage 22, the concave bearing surface aligns itself with the surface of the pipe 20 that it meets, and bears on the pipe over an area rather than along an edge. The split pipe clamp 10 therefore grips pipes over a range of diameters and does not require a tool specific pipe diameter. The pad axis is parallel to the axis of the pipe 20 in the illustrated form, and the jaw pad 26 may be faced with an elastomer, with a soft metal, or with a friction material where the pipe surface is to be protected.

A carriage spring 42 biases each jaw carriage 22 outward, away from the central axis of the closed frame. The carriage spring 42 may be a compression spring seated in the radial guide 24, a tension spring acting between the jaw carriage 22 and the frame, or a leaf element. When the releasable latch 18 is released, the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22 and lift the jaw pads 26 clear of the pipe 20, so that the frame halves can be swung apart without the jaw pads 26 dragging on the pipe.

The segmented cam ring

A cam ring 30 is retained in an annular guide 36 of the frame, as shown in FIG. 2. The annular guide 36 is an annular channel of the frame, concentric with the central axis of the closed frame, that locates the cam ring 30 radially and axially while allowing it to rotate through a limited stroke about that axis. Because the annular guide 36 continues around both frame halves, the reaction to the clamping load is taken by the frame around the whole arc rather than across the split line between the frame halves.

The mounting boss 66 stands on the frame radially outside the annular guide 36, clear of the cam ring 30 and of the jaw carriages 22.

The cam ring 30 is segmented. Referring to FIG. 3, the cam ring 30 comprises a first cam-ring segment 32 and a second cam-ring segment 34. The first cam-ring segment 32 is carried by the first frame half 12 and the second cam-ring segment 34 is carried by the second frame half 14, each segment being retained by the frame half that carries it. Each segment accordingly stays with its own frame half when the frame is opened, and the frame halves can be swung fully apart without dismantling the drive.

The first cam-ring segment 32 has a hinge-end drive face 44 and a latch-end drive face 48. The second cam-ring segment 34 has a hinge-end drive face 46 and a latch-end drive face 50. The hinge-end drive face 44 and the hinge-end drive face 46 are complementary to one another, and the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 are complementary to one another. Closing the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 at the hinge end and brings the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50 at the latch end, and thereby couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 so that they rotate together as one cam ring 30 about the central axis of the closed frame.

The complementary drive faces may be plain abutment faces lying in radial planes, faces inclined so that one segment end laps the other, or a tongue on one segment received in a recess of the other. What matters is that in the closed frame each pair of faces transmits circumferential drive from one segment to the other in the direction of the clamping stroke, and that the faces separate freely when the frame halves are swung apart. The coupling is made by the closing motion of the frame halves themselves, so no fastener, key or separate coupling action is required of the operator, and there is no state in which the frame is closed but the drive is not yet made up.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a follower 40 that is received in a respective oblique slot 38 of the cam ring 30, as shown in FIG. 2. The follower 40 may be a pin, a roller on a pin, or a block. Each oblique slot 38 is inclined to the circumferential direction of the cam ring 30, so that rotation of the cam ring 30 through the limited stroke displaces the follower 40, and with it the jaw carriage 22, along the radial guide 24. The oblique slots 38 are identical in inclination and are distributed to match the distribution of the jaw carriages 22, so that a single rotation of the cam ring 30 produces the same inward travel at every jaw carriage 22. Advance of the jaws is therefore synchronized by the geometry of the oblique slots 38 rather than by successive adjustment of individual jaws, and no jaw can be advanced independently of the others.

Where the pipe 20 is not exactly centred when the frame is closed, the jaw pad 26 that reaches the pipe first begins to centre the pipe within the frame, because the other jaw pads 26 continue to advance by the same amount until they too make contact. The inclination of the oblique slots 38 may be chosen to trade stroke against mechanical advantage, a shallower inclination giving a larger clamping force for a given drive force and a smaller radial travel for a given rotation, and the useful range of pipe diameters for a given clamp is set by the total radial travel available at the jaw carriages 22.

The latch drive

The releasable latch 18 carries a wedge 52, as shown in FIG. 4. Moving the releasable latch 18 drives the wedge 52 against a ring drive face 54 of the cam ring 30, shown in FIG. 3, and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke. The ring drive face 54 is presented at the latch end of the cam ring 30 and is inclined to the path of the wedge 52, so that advance of the wedge 52 is converted into circumferential displacement of the cam ring 30. The ring drive face 54 may be formed on a lug that projects outwardly from one of the cam-ring segments at the latch end, or on the end of a segment itself where the annular guide 36 is open to the wedge 52. The limited stroke is bounded by the frame, by the ends of the oblique slots 38, or by a stop face of the annular guide 36, so that the cam ring 30 cannot be driven beyond the working range of the jaw carriages 22.

The releasable latch 18 has a first position and a second position. In the first position the releasable latch 18 holds the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 closed around the pipe 20 without clamping the pipe 20, the cam ring 30 standing at the beginning of its stroke and the jaw carriages 22 remaining retracted under the carriage springs 42. The second position is an over-center position, in which the releasable latch 18 has driven the wedge 52 and the cam ring 30 and clamps the pipe 20, and in which the line of action of the clamping load passes over the pivot of the releasable latch 18 so that the load holds the latch closed rather than opening it. The first position allows the operator to capture the pipe 20 and slide or rotate the split pipe clamp 10 to its intended station before any clamping load is applied.

Referring again to FIG. 4, the releasable latch 18 comprises a latch handle 56, a latch housing 58 and an over-center link 68 connecting the latch handle 56 to the drive path that ends at the wedge 52. A force-limiting spring stack 62 lies in that drive path between the latch handle 56 and the wedge 52. The force-limiting spring stack 62 may be a stack of disc springs, a nest of helical compression springs, or a single compression spring, selected to a chosen preload and rate.

Until all of the jaw pads 26 have contacted the pipe 20, the force-limiting spring stack 62 transmits the drive from the latch handle 56 to the wedge 52 substantially without compressing, because the resistance of the retracting carriage springs 42 is small compared with the preload of the force-limiting spring stack 62. Once all of the jaw pads 26 have contacted the pipe 20, further movement of the latch handle 56 toward the over-center position compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than forcing one jaw pad 26 farther than the others. The additional latch travel that remains after contact, which varies from installation to installation with the diameter and the tolerance of the pipe 20, is therefore taken up elastically. The clamping load is set by the force-limiting spring stack 62 and not by the position at which the releasable latch 18 comes to rest, so the same clamp applies a comparable load to a large pipe and to a small pipe within its range, and a thin walled pipe is not deformed by the surplus travel of the latch.

An indicator pin 64 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 62 and moves relative to a fixed edge 60 of the latch housing 58 when the force-limiting spring stack 62 enters a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 64 is carried by the movable end of the force-limiting spring stack 62 and projects through an opening of the latch housing 58, so that its position relative to the fixed edge 60 follows the compression of the force-limiting spring stack 62. The predetermined compression range corresponds to the intended clamping load of the split pipe clamp 10, and the emergence of the indicator pin 64 past the fixed edge 60 is a visible mechanical report that the clamp is loaded within that range. The indicator pin 64 reports clamp loading and does not measure the diameter of the pipe 20. No electrical power, instrumentation or calibration equipment is required at the pipe to read it, and the report is available at the moment the latch is closed.

Installation and removal

To install the split pipe clamp 10, an operator opens the releasable latch 18 and swings the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 20 and closes them, which brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 and the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50, and so couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 into a single cam ring 30. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the first position, in which the frame halves are held around the pipe 20 without clamping, and positions the split pipe clamp 10 along the pipe 20. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the over-center position. The wedge 52 bears on the ring drive face 54 and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke, the oblique slots 38 advance all of the jaw carriages 22 inward together, and the jaw pads 26 pivot and seat on the pipe 20. Remaining travel of the latch handle 56 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the operator confirms the clamping load by observing the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60.

To remove the split pipe clamp 10, the operator releases the releasable latch 18. The force-limiting spring stack 62 unloads, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 54, and the carriage springs 42 rotate the cam ring 30 back through the oblique slots 38 and retract the jaw carriages 22, lifting the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are then swung apart about the hinge 16, and the hinge-end drive face 44, the hinge-end drive face 46, the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 separate so that the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 travel with their own frame halves. The split pipe clamp 10 is reusable and may be fitted, removed and refitted without tools.

The essential relationship of the arrangement described here is that closure of the frame halves couples the cam-ring segments, that travel of the releasable latch 18 drives the coupled cam ring 30, that the oblique slots 38 synchronize the radial travel of the jaw carriages 22, and that the force-limiting spring stack 62 accommodates the remaining latch travel. The features described above may be combined in ways other than those expressly set out, and modifications within the understanding of a person skilled in the art fall within the scope of the claims that follow.

In the first position the releasable latch 18 holds the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 closed around the pipe 20 without clamping the pipe 20, the cam ring 30 standing at the beginning of its stroke and the jaw carriages 22 remaining retracted under the carriage springs 42. The second position is an over-center position, in which the releasable latch 18 has driven the wedge 52 and the cam ring 30 and clamps the pipe 20, and in which the line of action of the clamping load passes over the pivot of the releasable latch 18 so that the load holds the latch closed rather than opening it. The first position allows the operator to capture the pipe 20 and slide or rotate the split pipe clamp 10 to its intended station before any clamping load is applied.

-Referring again to FIG. 4, the releasable latch 18 comprises a latch handle 56, a latch housing 58 and an over-center link 68 connecting the latch handle 56 to the drive path that ends at the wedge 52. A force-limiting spring stack 62 lies in that drive path between the latch handle 56 and the wedge 52. The force-limiting spring stack 62 may be a stack of disc springs, a nest of helical compression springs, or a single compression spring, selected to a chosen preload and rate.

+Referring again to FIG. 4, the releasable latch 18 comprises a latch handle 56, a latch housing 58, a force-limiting spring stack 62 and an over-center link 68. The force-limiting spring stack 62 lies in a drive path between the latch handle 56 and the wedge 52, and the over-center link 68 connects the latch handle 56 to the force-limiting spring stack 62. The force-limiting spring stack 62 may be a stack of disc springs, a nest of helical compression springs, or a single compression spring, selected to a chosen preload and rate.

Until all of the jaw pads 26 have contacted the pipe 20, the force-limiting spring stack 62 transmits the drive from the latch handle 56 to the wedge 52 substantially without compressing, because the resistance of the carriage springs 42 is small compared with the preload of the force-limiting spring stack 62. Once all of the jaw pads 26 have contacted the pipe 20, further movement of the latch handle 56 toward the over-center position compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than forcing one jaw pad 26 farther than the others. The additional latch travel that remains after contact, which varies from installation to installation with the diameter and the tolerance of the pipe 20, is therefore taken up elastically. The clamping load is set by the force-limiting spring stack 62 and not by the position at which the releasable latch 18 comes to rest, so the same clamp applies a comparable load to a large pipe and to a small pipe within its range, and a thin walled pipe is not deformed by the surplus travel of the latch.

input.summary: Wrote the complete first draft of the split pipe clamp application: all ten body sections, the reference-numeral table, and four figure briefs (assembly elevation, frame interior showing the cam drive, the segmented cam ring alone, and a cutaway of the force-limited latch). Claim set is 24 claims in three statutory groupings: an apparatus independent (claim 1), an installed-assembly independent (claim 16), and a method independent (claim 19), with a graduated dependent ladder under each. Important caveat on prior art: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and the brief states that no prior-art search was run, so this draft was written with no art to design around and contains no citations. The art you were given may be incomplete, and claim 1 has not been tested against any real reference; a search should be run before filing and claim 1 may need narrowing, most naturally by pulling up the force-limiting spring stack from claim 2.
reasoning: Claim 1 is built around the one relationship the disclosure calls essential and that is structurally unusual: the cam ring is itself split, one segment travels with each frame half, and the act of closing the frame brings complementary drive faces at both the hinge end and the latch end into engagement so the two segments rotate as a single ring. That is what lets a split frame drive a full-circle cam without the operator making up a coupling, and it is the feature that would carry the claim clear of ordinary hinged band or bolted split clamps, whose tightening motion runs through the split line.

I kept the force-limiting spring stack and the indicator pin OUT of claim 1 deliberately. They are strong, arguable features, but a competitor who copies the segmented-ring-coupled-by-closure drive with a rigid latch would still infringe claim 1 as written; putting the spring stack in claim 1 would hand that away. The stack is claim 2, the indicator is claim 3, and both are recited in independent claim 16, so if claim 1 falls there is a fallback that is still worth having and an independent claim that already carries them.

Claim 1 recites 'a plurality of jaw carriages' rather than 'three'. The disclosure only names three, so I added a passage to the detailed description explaining that three is the illustrated form and that each additional carriage is coupled by its own follower and its own oblique slot in the same manner. That is a functional generalization of the disclosed mechanism, not a new fact, and it supports the plurality language; claim 7 falls back to exactly three.

Claim 16 is an installed assembly (pipe plus clamp), which is infringed by the installer rather than the manufacturer, and claim 19 is the installation method taken directly from the operator sequence in the disclosure. I did not draft a method-of-manufacture claim: the disclosure says nothing about how the parts are made or assembled, so any such claim would have needed invented process steps.

The over-center latch needed a linkage to be enabled. The disclosure gives the handle, the wedge, the spring stack between them, the two latch positions and the indicator pin, so I described the connection as an over-center link and gave it a numeral, described the spring stack alternatives functionally (disc spring stack, nest of helical springs, single compression spring), and avoided inventing a keeper, a latch pivot pin or any specific geometry. No values, angles, spring rates or dimensions appear anywhere.

The Background sets up three technical problems in advance of any argument that may later be needed: grip concentrated at the split line when the halves are drawn together, jaws wound in one at a time pushing the pipe off axis, and a quick latch giving the operator no report of load. The Detailed Description then states what each disclosed feature does about each problem, including why the annular guide keeps the reaction off the split line and why the spring stack bounds the load independently of where the latch stops.

Figures: FIG. 2 had to be split from FIG. 3 because the carriage drive and the segment coupling together exceed the eight-numeral sheet limit. FIG. 3 shows the ring alone so both junctions and all four drive faces are visible on one sheet, which no in-frame view could do. FIG. 1's brief therefore names the cam ring only as an unnumbered band and FIG. 2's brief does not use the segment part names. To ground FIG. 3's lug, I added a 'may be formed on a lug, or on the end of a segment' alternative to the description rather than letting the drawing dictate a structure the text did not carry.

Claim 8 was rewritten from 'two in the first half, one in the second' to 'two in one half, a remaining one in the other' so it matches the description and does not conflict with the carriage positions shown in FIG. 1, and claim 10 was rewritten to say each segment remains carried by its own frame half, since 'the annular guide of the first frame half' had no antecedent in claim 1.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/ contains only INDEX.md, and its table lists no references; the drafting brief confirms that no prior-art search was run. There was therefore nothing to read, nothing to cite, and no reference whose combination could be checked against the claims. The draft contains no [REF:] citations, since citing a key not in the index is prohibited, and the Background makes only general statements about the kinds of split clamp construction the invention departs from, without attributing them to any document. In place of art-driven design-around, I made claim 1 turn on the most concrete and least conventional relationship in the disclosure: a cam ring split into segments that are carried individually by the two frame halves and are coupled into a single rotating ring by the closing motion of the frame itself, with a latch-borne wedge acting on a ring drive face and oblique slots converting that one rotation into equal inward travel at every jaw carriage. The specification states, before it is needed, the technical problem that combination solves, namely that the clamping reaction is taken by the annular guide around the whole arc instead of across the split line, and that jaw advance is fixed by slot geometry instead of by operator judgment. The reserve position is the force-limiting spring stack with its mechanical load indicator, held in claims 2, 3 and 16 to 17. This strategy should be revisited once a search has been run; the claims have not been tested against any actual reference.

content:
The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.

1	A reusable split pipe clamp has two frame halves joined at a hinge end by a hinge and at a latch end by a releasable latch, so the frame opens around a pipe already in place. Jaw carriages distributed about the frame slide in radial guides and carry pivoting jaw pads having concave bearing surfaces. A cam ring in an annular guide is segmented, one segment travelling with each frame half, and complementary drive faces at the hinge end and the latch end couple the segments into one rotating ring when the frame closes. A wedge on the latch bears on a ring drive face and turns the coupled ring through a limited stroke, and oblique slots acting on followers advance all jaw carriages inward together. A force-limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge absorbs remaining latch travel, and an indicator pin moving relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing reports clamping load.

In the following description, like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views. The described arrangement is one form of the invention and is not a limitation on the scope of the claims. Terms of orientation such as inward, outward, radial and circumferential are used with reference to a central axis of the closed frame, which in use is substantially coincident with the axis of the pipe being gripped.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a split pipe clamp 10 comprises a first frame half 12 and a second frame half 14. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are each substantially semicircular, and together they define a frame that surrounds a pipe 20 when closed. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are joined at a hinge end of the frame by a hinge 16 and are releasably joined at a latch end of the frame, opposite the hinge end, by a releasable latch 18. Swinging the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16 opens the frame laterally, so that the split pipe clamp 10 can be applied to a pipe 20 that is already installed and that cannot be entered from a free end. The split pipe clamp 10 and the pipe 20 together form an installed clamp assembly when the split pipe clamp 10 is closed and clamped on the pipe 20.

Three jaw carriages 22 are distributed circumferentially about the closed frame, as shown in FIG. 1.

The frame carries a mounting boss 66. The mounting boss 66 supports a sensor, a tool or a conduit on the split pipe clamp 10. The mounting boss 66 does not participate in advancing or synchronizing the jaw carriages 22.

Jaw carriages and jaw pads

Referring to FIG. 2, each jaw carriage 22 is slidable in a respective radial guide 24 of the frame. The radial guide 24 constrains the jaw carriage 22 to travel along a radial path toward and away from the central axis of the closed frame.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a jaw pad 26 that is mounted on the jaw carriage 22 for pivoting movement and that presents a concave bearing surface toward the central axis of the closed frame. Because the jaw pad 26 pivots relative to the jaw carriage 22, the jaw pad 26 bears on the pipe 20 without requiring a tool specific pipe diameter.

A carriage spring 42 biases each jaw carriage 22 outward, away from the central axis of the closed frame. When the releasable latch 18 is released, the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22 outward and lift the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened.

The segmented cam ring

A cam ring 30 is retained in an annular guide 36 of the frame, as shown in FIG. 2. The annular guide 36 is an annular channel of the frame, concentric with the central axis of the closed frame, that retains the cam ring 30 while allowing the cam ring 30 to rotate through a limited stroke about that axis.

The mounting boss 66 stands on the frame outside the annular guide 36, clear of the cam ring 30 and of the jaw carriages 22.

The cam ring 30 is segmented. Referring to FIG. 3, the cam ring 30 comprises a first cam-ring segment 32 and a second cam-ring segment 34. The first cam-ring segment 32 is carried by the first frame half 12 and the second cam-ring segment 34 is carried by the second frame half 14, each segment being retained by the frame half that carries it. Each segment accordingly stays with its own frame half when the frame is opened, and the frame halves can be swung apart without dismantling the drive.

The first cam-ring segment 32 has a hinge-end drive face 44 and a latch-end drive face 48. The second cam-ring segment 34 has a hinge-end drive face 46 and a latch-end drive face 50. The hinge-end drive face 44 and the hinge-end drive face 46 are complementary to one another, and the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 are complementary to one another. Closing the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 at the hinge end and brings the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50 at the latch end, and thereby couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 so that they rotate together as one cam ring 30 about the central axis of the closed frame.

In the closed frame each pair of complementary drive faces transmits circumferential drive from one cam-ring segment to the other, and the complementary drive faces separate when the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are swung apart about the hinge 16.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a follower 40 that is received in a respective oblique slot 38 of the cam ring 30, as shown in FIG. 2. Each oblique slot 38 is inclined to the circumferential direction of the cam ring 30, so that rotation of the cam ring 30 through the limited stroke displaces the follower 40, and with it the jaw carriage 22, along the radial guide 24. The oblique slots 38 are identical in inclination and are distributed circumferentially to match the jaw carriages 22, so that rotation of the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke produces the same inward travel at every jaw carriage 22. The inward travel of the three jaw carriages 22 is thereby synchronized.

The latch drive

The releasable latch 18 carries a wedge 52, as shown in FIG. 4. Moving the releasable latch 18 drives the wedge 52 against a ring drive face 54 of the cam ring 30, shown in FIG. 3, and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke.

The releasable latch 18 has a first position and a second position. In the first position the releasable latch 18 holds the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 around the pipe 20 without clamping the pipe 20. The second position is an over-center position, in which the releasable latch 18 has driven the wedge 52 and the cam ring 30 and clamps the pipe 20.

Referring again to FIG. 4, the releasable latch 18 comprises a latch handle 56, a latch housing 58 and a force-limiting spring stack 62. The force-limiting spring stack 62 lies in a drive path between the latch handle 56 and the wedge 52.

Once all of the jaw pads 26 have contacted the pipe 20, further movement of the latch handle 56 toward the over-center position compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than forcing one jaw pad 26 farther than the others. The latch travel that remains after contact is therefore taken up by the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the clamping load is set by the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than by the position at which the releasable latch 18 comes to rest.

An indicator pin 64 is visible on the releasable latch 18 and moves relative to a fixed edge 60 of the latch housing 58 when the force-limiting spring stack 62 enters a predetermined compression range. The position of the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60 is a mechanical report that the split pipe clamp 10 is loaded within that range. The indicator pin 64 reports clamp loading and does not measure the diameter of the pipe 20.

Installation and removal

To install the split pipe clamp 10, an operator opens the releasable latch 18 and swings the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 20 and closes them, which brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 and the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50, and so couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 into a single cam ring 30. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the first position, in which the frame halves are held around the pipe 20 without clamping. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the over-center position. The wedge 52 bears on the ring drive face 54 and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke, the oblique slots 38 advance all of the jaw carriages 22 inward together, and the jaw pads 26 pivot and seat on the pipe 20. Latch travel remaining after the jaw pads 26 seat compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the operator observes the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60.

To remove the split pipe clamp 10, the operator releases the releasable latch 18. The force-limiting spring stack 62 unloads and the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22, lifting the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are then swung apart about the hinge 16, and the hinge-end drive face 44, the hinge-end drive face 46, the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 separate so that the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 travel with their own frame halves. The split pipe clamp 10 is reusable.

The essential relationship of the arrangement described here is that closure of the frame halves couples the cam-ring segments, that travel of the releasable latch 18 drives the coupled cam ring 30, that the oblique slots 38 synchronize the radial travel of the jaw carriages 22, and that the force-limiting spring stack 62 accommodates the remaining latch travel. The features described above may be combined in ways other than those expressly set out, and modifications within the understanding of a person skilled in the art fall within the scope of the claims that follow.

Referring to FIG. 1, a split pipe clamp 10 comprises a first frame half 12 and a second frame half 14. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are each substantially semicircular, and together they define a frame that surrounds a pipe 20 when closed. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are joined at a hinge end of the frame by a hinge 16 and are releasably joined at a latch end of the frame, opposite the hinge end, by a releasable latch 18. Swinging the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16 opens the frame laterally, so that the split pipe clamp 10 can be applied to a pipe 20 that is already installed and that cannot be entered from a free end. The split pipe clamp 10 and the pipe 20 together form an installed clamp assembly when the split pipe clamp 10 is closed and clamped on the pipe 20.

Three jaw carriages 22 are distributed circumferentially about the closed frame, as shown in FIG. 1.

The frame carries a mounting boss 66. The mounting boss 66 supports a sensor, a tool or a conduit on the split pipe clamp 10. The mounting boss 66 does not participate in advancing or synchronizing the jaw carriages 22.

Jaw carriages and jaw pads

Referring to FIG. 2, each jaw carriage 22 is slidable in a respective radial guide 24 of the frame. The radial guide 24 constrains the jaw carriage 22 to travel along a radial path toward and away from the central axis of the closed frame.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a jaw pad 26 that is mounted on the jaw carriage 22 for pivoting movement and that presents a concave bearing surface toward the central axis of the closed frame. Because the jaw pad 26 pivots relative to the jaw carriage 22, the jaw pad 26 bears on the pipe 20 without requiring a tool specific pipe diameter.

A carriage spring 42 biases each jaw carriage 22 outward, away from the central axis of the closed frame. When the releasable latch 18 is released, the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22 outward and lift the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened.

The segmented cam ring

A cam ring 30 is retained in an annular guide 36 of the frame, as shown in FIG. 2. The annular guide 36 is an annular channel of the frame, concentric with the central axis of the closed frame, that retains the cam ring 30 while allowing the cam ring 30 to rotate through a limited stroke about that axis.

The mounting boss 66 stands on the frame outside the annular guide 36, clear of the cam ring 30 and of the jaw carriages 22.

The cam ring 30 is segmented. Referring to FIG. 3, the cam ring 30 comprises a first cam-ring segment 32 and a second cam-ring segment 34. The first cam-ring segment 32 is carried by the first frame half 12 and the second cam-ring segment 34 is carried by the second frame half 14, each segment being retained by the frame half that carries it. Each segment accordingly stays with its own frame half when the frame is opened, and the frame halves can be swung apart without dismantling the drive.

The first cam-ring segment 32 has a hinge-end drive face 44 and a latch-end drive face 48. The second cam-ring segment 34 has a hinge-end drive face 46 and a latch-end drive face 50. The hinge-end drive face 44 and the hinge-end drive face 46 are complementary to one another, and the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 are complementary to one another. Closing the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 at the hinge end and brings the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50 at the latch end, and thereby couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 so that they rotate together as one cam ring 30 about the central axis of the closed frame.

In the closed frame each pair of complementary drive faces transmits circumferential drive from one cam-ring segment to the other, and the complementary drive faces separate when the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are swung apart about the hinge 16.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a follower 40 that is received in a respective oblique slot 38 of the cam ring 30, as shown in FIG. 2. Each oblique slot 38 is inclined to the circumferential direction of the cam ring 30, so that rotation of the cam ring 30 through the limited stroke displaces the follower 40, and with it the jaw carriage 22, along the radial guide 24. The oblique slots 38 are identical in inclination and are distributed circumferentially to match the jaw carriages 22, so that rotation of the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke produces the same inward travel at every jaw carriage 22. The inward travel of the three jaw carriages 22 is thereby synchronized.

The latch drive

The releasable latch 18 carries a wedge 52, as shown in FIG. 4. Moving the releasable latch 18 drives the wedge 52 against a ring drive face 54 of the cam ring 30, shown in FIG. 3, and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke.

The releasable latch 18 has a first position and a second position. In the first position the releasable latch 18 holds the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 around the pipe 20 without clamping the pipe 20. The second position is an over-center position, in which the releasable latch 18 has driven the wedge 52 and the cam ring 30 and clamps the pipe 20.

Referring again to FIG. 4, the releasable latch 18 comprises a latch handle 56, a latch housing 58 and a force-limiting spring stack 62. The force-limiting spring stack 62 lies in a drive path between the latch handle 56 and the wedge 52.

Once all of the jaw pads 26 have contacted the pipe 20, further movement of the latch handle 56 toward the over-center position compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than forcing one jaw pad 26 farther than the others. The latch travel that remains after contact is therefore taken up by the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the clamping load is set by the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than by the position at which the releasable latch 18 comes to rest.

An indicator pin 64 is visible on the releasable latch 18 and moves relative to a fixed edge 60 of the latch housing 58 when the force-limiting spring stack 62 enters a predetermined compression range. The position of the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60 is a mechanical report that the split pipe clamp 10 is loaded within that range. The indicator pin 64 reports clamp loading and does not measure the diameter of the pipe 20.

Installation and removal

To install the split pipe clamp 10, an operator opens the releasable latch 18 and swings the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 20 and closes them, which brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 and the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50, and so couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 into a single cam ring 30. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the first position, in which the frame halves are held around the pipe 20 without clamping. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the over-center position. The wedge 52 bears on the ring drive face 54 and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke, the oblique slots 38 advance all of the jaw carriages 22 inward together, and the jaw pads 26 pivot and seat on the pipe 20. Latch travel remaining after the jaw pads 26 seat compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the operator observes the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60.

To remove the split pipe clamp 10, the operator releases the releasable latch 18. The force-limiting spring stack 62 unloads and the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22, lifting the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are then swung apart about the hinge 16, and the hinge-end drive face 44, the hinge-end drive face 46, the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 separate so that the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 travel with their own frame halves. The split pipe clamp 10 is reusable.

The essential relationship of the arrangement described here is that closure of the frame halves couples the cam-ring segments, that travel of the releasable latch 18 drives the coupled cam ring 30, that the oblique slots 38 synchronize the radial travel of the jaw carriages 22, and that the force-limiting spring stack 62 accommodates the remaining latch travel. The features described above may be combined in ways other than those expressly set out, and modifications within the understanding of a person skilled in the art fall within the scope of the claims that follow.

input.content:
A reusable split pipe clamp is disclosed in which the cam ring that advances the jaws is itself split, one segment travelling with each half of the frame, and is made into a working ring by the act of closing the frame.

The clamp has a first frame half and a second frame half joined at a hinge end by a hinge and joined at a latch end by a releasable latch, so that the frame halves can be swung apart, placed around a pipe that is already installed, and closed again. Three jaw carriages are distributed circumferentially about the closed frame. Each jaw carriage is slidable in a radial guide of the frame and carries a jaw pad that is mounted on the jaw carriage for pivoting movement and that presents a concave bearing surface to the pipe. Because each jaw pad pivots, it bears on the pipe without requiring a tool specific pipe diameter.

A cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame. The cam ring is segmented. A first cam-ring segment is carried by the first frame half and a second cam-ring segment is carried by the second frame half, so each segment stays with its own frame half when the clamp is opened. The first cam-ring segment and the second cam-ring segment have complementary drive faces at the hinge end and complementary drive faces at the latch end. Closing the frame halves brings those complementary drive faces into engagement and couples the cam-ring segments so that they move together as one cam ring about the pipe, and the faces separate again when the frame halves are swung apart.

Each jaw carriage carries a follower that is received in a respective oblique slot of the cam ring. The latch carries a wedge. Moving the latch drives the wedge against a ring drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled cam ring through a limited stroke about the pipe. The oblique slots are identical in inclination and are distributed circumferentially to match the jaw carriages, so that the common rotation of the cam ring produces the same inward travel at every jaw carriage and the inward travel of the three jaw carriages is synchronized. A carriage spring biases each jaw carriage outward, so that releasing the latch retracts the jaw carriages and lifts the jaw pads off the pipe before the frame halves are opened.

The latch has a first position in which it holds the frame halves around the pipe without clamping and a second, over-center position in which it drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe. The two positions separate the act of capturing the pipe from the act of loading the jaws.

A force-limiting spring stack lies in the drive path between a latch handle of the latch and the wedge. Once all of the jaw pads have contacted the pipe, further travel of the latch handle toward the over-center position is absorbed by compression of the force-limiting spring stack instead of forcing one jaw pad farther than the others. The latch travel that remains after contact is therefore taken up by the force-limiting spring stack, and the clamping load is set by that spring stack rather than by the position at which the latch comes to rest.

An indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of a latch housing of the latch when the force-limiting spring stack enters a predetermined compression range, so that the position of the indicator pin relative to that fixed edge reports mechanically that the clamp is loaded within the range. The indicator reports clamp loading and does not measure pipe diameter.

Pipework in process plants, buildings, vehicles and drilling installations frequently has to be gripped by a device that cannot be threaded on from a free end of the pipe. Sensors, monitoring heads, marking tools, small actuators and conduit supports all have to be attached to a run of pipe that is already installed and often still in service. A clamp intended for that duty is therefore built as a split clamp: a frame that opens, is placed around the pipe transversely, and is closed again.

A split frame creates a mechanical difficulty that a one piece collar does not have. The tightening motion has to be delivered across the split line. Where the two frame halves are drawn toward one another so that the frame itself shrinks onto the pipe, the closing force enters the frame at the split line, and the grip the pipe feels depends on the closure hardware and on where around the arc the pipe is touched. When the clamp is meant to hold a measuring head in a repeatable position, a grip that varies in that way is a source of error, and repeated opening and closing need not return the head to the same place.

Where the frame is instead fitted with individually adjustable jaws or screws that are wound in against the pipe one at a time, the grip is separated from the split line, but a tool is needed, the operator has to balance the jaws by feel, and the work is slow. If one jaw is advanced further than the others, the pipe is pushed off the axis of the frame, and the clamp is again seated differently each time it is fitted.

Clamps of both kinds are commonly sized for a nominal pipe diameter, so a technician has to carry a set of clamps and identify the correct one before working. A jaw face that is flat, or curved to one nominal diameter, meets a pipe of another diameter along an edge rather than over an area.

An operator working with a quick acting latch also has little to go on in judging how hard the clamp has been applied. A latch that snaps shut can feel much the same whether the jaws have seated properly on the pipe, whether the pipe is at the small end of the range and the jaws have barely reached it, or whether the mechanism has been travelled too far. Torque measurement is available for a bolted clamp but not for a latch, and a diameter reading indicates the size of the pipe rather than the load the clamp is carrying.

There is accordingly a need for a split pipe clamp that can be fitted by hand around an in place pipe of a range of diameters, that advances several jaws onto the pipe together rather than one at a time, and that reports mechanically when the clamping load has reached the intended range.

# FIG. 1

View: front elevation of the clamp closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Patent line drawing, black line work on white, no shading or color. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

Geometry to draw:

- A circular pipe drawn as one plain circle at the center of the drawing area, occupying roughly the middle third of the drawing area width. Its interior is empty.
- Around that circle, an annular frame body drawn as an outer boundary and an inner boundary, concentric with the pipe circle and spaced outward from it, so a band of frame material surrounds the pipe. The annular frame body is divided into two substantially semicircular halves by two radial breaks, one at the left of the ring and one at the right of the ring. The upper half and the lower half are drawn as separate solids meeting at those breaks.
- At the left break, a hinge drawn as a small circle straddling the two halves, with a short pair of straight lines joining it to each half, so the halves are visibly pivoted together there.
- At the right break, a latch drawn as a compact rectangular body attached across the two halves and overlapping both, with a straight lever arm extending from it outward and downward to the right.
- Three carriage blocks spaced around the annulus at roughly equal angular intervals, one at the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, none of them at the left break or the right break. Each is a small rectangle whose long dimension is radial, passing through the inner boundary of the annular frame body and stopping short of the pipe circle.
- Between the inner end of each carriage block and the pipe circle, a small block whose inner edge is a concave arc that meets the pipe circle, so that this small block, and not the carriage block, contacts the pipe.
- A mounting boss drawn as a small rectangular pad standing on the outer boundary of the annular frame body at the upper right, projecting radially outward and joined to it.

The hinge, the latch, the small blocks at the inner ends of the carriage blocks, and the mounting boss are shown schematically.

Reference numerals appearing on this sheet: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 66.

Numeral targets:

- 10: the outer boundary line of the annular frame body at the lower left, identifying the assembly as a whole.
- 12: well inside the upper half of the annular frame body, toward the top.
- 14: well inside the lower half of the annular frame body, toward the bottom.
- 16: the small circle at the left break.
- 18: well inside the compact rectangular latch body at the right break.
- 20: the interior of the pipe circle.
- 22: well inside the carriage block at the top of the ring.
- 66: well inside the rectangular pad at the upper right.

# FIG. 2

View: front interior view of the closed clamp along the pipe axis. Patent line drawing, black line work on white, no shading or color. Near side frame material is omitted so the interior is open to view, which is a depiction convention. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

Geometry to draw:

- An annular body drawn as concentric outer and inner boundary circles centered in the drawing area. The space between them is open, without hatching, and the region inside the inner circle is empty. No pipe is drawn.
- Within that space, a narrow band drawn as two concentric arcs set toward the outer boundary. This band is the cam ring, divided at two diametrically opposite locations, one left and one right, each division drawn as a short line across the width of the band.
- Outboard of the band, a channel outline of two further concentric arcs between the band and the outer circle, so the band sits in that channel, drawn in the three arc stretches between the slideways.
- Three slideways through the annular body at roughly equal angular intervals, one at the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, none at either division. Each is a pair of parallel straight lines running radially between the two boundary circles.
- In each slideway a carriage drawn as a radially long rectangle, narrower than the slideway so the guide lines stay visible on both sides. Each carriage stops short of the inner circle and its outer end reaches the band.
- On the inner end of each carriage a pad drawn as a small block whose inner edge is a concave arc curving away from the center of the view, joined to the carriage at a small circle.
- At the outer end of each carriage a small circle representing a follower, lying on the band, and around it a slot drawn as an elongated closed outline through the band, inclined so its long direction is neither purely radial nor purely along the band. The three slots share one rotational sense.
- In the outer stretch of each slideway, between the carriage and the outer circle, a spring drawn as a short zigzag line.

The cam ring, followers and springs are shown schematically.

Reference numerals appearing on this sheet: 22, 24, 26, 30, 36, 38, 40, 42.

Numeral targets:

- 22: well inside the carriage rectangle at the top.
- 24: a guide line of the lower left slideway.
- 26: well inside the pad block at the lower right.
- 30: well inside the band at the lower left, clear of any slot.
- 36: the channel outline at the upper right.
- 38: the slot outline at the lower left, clear of the follower circle in it.
- 40: the follower circle at the top.
- 42: the zigzag spring at the lower right.

# FIG. 3

View: plan view of the cam ring alone, removed from the frame and viewed along its axis. Patent line drawing, black line work on white, no shading or color. The ring is drawn as it stands when the frame halves are closed, so its two segments are shown end to end. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

Geometry to draw:

- A ring drawn as two concentric circles centered in the drawing area, forming a band of uniform width that occupies the middle of the drawing area. The region inside the inner circle is empty.
- The band is divided into an upper arcuate segment and a lower arcuate segment by two junctions, one at the left and one at the right. At each junction the end face of the upper segment and the end face of the lower segment are two short faces of matching outline that meet across the width of the band, so the two segments read as separate solids in contact. The shape of these end faces is shown schematically.
- On the outer side of the band, between the right junction and the slot at the lower right, a short plain drive face drawn on the outer boundary of the band, shown schematically.
- Three elongated closed slot outlines through the band, spaced at roughly equal angular intervals and clear of both junctions: one near the top of the band, one at the lower left of the band and one at the lower right of the band. Each slot is inclined so that its long direction runs neither purely radially nor purely along the band, and the three slots are inclined in the same rotational sense.

Reference numerals appearing on this sheet: 30, 32, 34, 44, 46, 48, 50, 54.

Numeral targets:

- 30: the outer circle of the band at the upper right, identifying the ring as a whole.
- 32: well inside the band at the upper left, between the left junction and the slot near the top.
- 34: well inside the band at the bottom, between the two lower slots.
- 44: the end face of the upper segment at the left junction.
- 46: the end face of the lower segment at the left junction.
- 48: the end face of the upper segment at the right junction.
- 50: the end face of the lower segment at the right junction.
- 54: the short plain drive face on the outer boundary of the band, between the right junction and the slot at the lower right.

# FIG. 1

View: front elevation of the clamp closed around a pipe, along the pipe axis. Patent line drawing, black line work on white, no shading or color. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

Geometry to draw:

- A pipe drawn as one plain circle at the center of the drawing area, occupying roughly the middle third of its width. The interior of the circle is empty.
- Around that circle, an annular frame body drawn as an outer boundary and an inner boundary, concentric with the pipe circle and spaced outward from it, so a band of frame material surrounds the pipe. It is divided into two substantially semicircular halves by two radial breaks, one at the left and one at the right, the upper half and the lower half being drawn as separate solids meeting at those breaks.
- At the left break, a hinge drawn as a small circle straddling the two halves, with a short pair of straight lines joining it to each half, so the halves are visibly pivoted together there.
- At the right break, a latch drawn as a compact rectangular body attached across the two halves and overlapping both, with a straight lever arm extending outward and downward to the right.
- Three carriage blocks at roughly equal angular intervals, one at the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, none of them at either break. Each is a small rectangle whose long dimension is radial, passing through the inner boundary of the annular frame body and stopping short of the pipe circle.
- Between the inner end of each carriage block and the pipe circle, a small block whose inner edge is a concave arc meeting the pipe circle, so that this small block, and not the carriage block, contacts the pipe.
- A mounting boss drawn as a small rectangular pad standing on the outer boundary of the annular frame body at the upper right, projecting radially outward and joined to it.

1	A reusable split pipe clamp is disclosed in which the tightening motion is not transmitted through the split line of the frame but through a cam ring that is itself split, and which is reassembled into a working ring by the act of closing the frame.
2	
3	The clamp has a first frame half and a second frame half joined at a hinge end by a hinge and joined at a latch end by a releasable latch, so that the frame halves can be swung apart, placed around a pipe that is already installed, and closed again. A plurality of jaw carriages is distributed circumferentially about the closed frame. Each jaw carriage is slidable in a radial guide of the frame and carries a jaw pad that is mounted on the jaw carriage for pivoting movement and that presents a concave bearing surface to the pipe. Because each jaw pad pivots, it seats itself on the pipe surface it meets, and the clamp is not restricted to one nominal pipe diameter.
4	
5	A cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame. The cam ring is segmented. A first cam-ring segment is carried by the first frame half and a second cam-ring segment is carried by the second frame half, so each segment stays with its own frame half when the clamp is opened. The first cam-ring segment and the second cam-ring segment have complementary drive faces at the hinge end and complementary drive faces at the latch end. Closing the frame halves brings those complementary drive faces into engagement and couples the cam-ring segments so that they move together as one cam ring about the pipe. Closure of the frame is therefore what creates the drive train, and no separate coupling step is asked of the operator.
6	
7	Each jaw carriage carries a follower that is received in a respective oblique slot of the cam ring. The latch carries a wedge. Moving the latch drives the wedge against a ring drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled cam ring through a limited stroke about the pipe. Each oblique slot converts that common rotation into inward travel of its own jaw carriage, so that all of the jaw carriages advance together by an amount fixed by the geometry of the slots rather than by the judgment of the operator. A carriage spring biases each jaw carriage outward, so that releasing the latch retracts the jaws before the frame halves are opened. The clamping load is taken by the cam ring in the annular guide rather than across the split line, and the latch is not asked to hold the working load through the frame joint.
8	
9	The latch has a first position in which it holds the frame halves around the pipe without clamping and a second, over-center position in which it drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe. The two positions separate the act of capturing the pipe from the act of loading the jaws, so the operator can position the clamp along the pipe while the frame is already captive.
10	
11	A force-limiting spring stack lies in the drive path between a latch handle of the latch and the wedge. Once all of the jaw pads have contacted the pipe, further travel of the latch handle to the over-center position is absorbed by compression of the force-limiting spring stack instead of forcing one jaw farther than the others. The remaining latch travel is therefore taken up by a defined elastic element, the clamping load is bounded by that element, and a pipe that sits anywhere within the range of the clamp is gripped by a load set by the spring stack rather than by where the latch happens to reach its stop.
12	
13	An indicator pin coupled to the force-limiting spring stack moves relative to a fixed edge of a latch housing of the latch when the force-limiting spring stack enters a predetermined compression range, giving the operator a visible mechanical report that the clamp is loaded within that range. The indicator reports clamp loading and does not measure pipe diameter.
14	
15	The frame may carry a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, a tool or a conduit. The mounting boss does not participate in advancing or synchronizing the jaw carriages, so a load applied to the mounting boss is carried by the frame and does not disturb the cam drive.
16	
17	A method of clamping a pipe and a method of releasing the clamp are also disclosed, in which the frame halves are closed about the pipe to couple the cam-ring segments, the latch is moved to the first position and then to the over-center position to rotate the coupled cam ring, and the residual latch travel is absorbed in the force-limiting spring stack.

1	In the following description, like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views. The described arrangement is one form of the invention and is not a limitation on the scope of the claims. Terms of orientation such as inward, outward, radial and circumferential are used with reference to a central axis of the closed frame, which in use is substantially coincident with the axis of the pipe being gripped.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	Referring to FIG. 1, a split pipe clamp 10 comprises a first frame half 12 and a second frame half 14. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are each substantially semicircular, and together they define a frame that surrounds a pipe 20 when the clamp is closed. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are joined at a hinge end of the frame by a hinge 16 and are releasably joined at a latch end of the frame, opposite the hinge end, by a releasable latch 18. Swinging the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16 opens the frame laterally, so that the split pipe clamp 10 can be applied to a pipe 20 that is already installed and that cannot be entered from a free end.
6	
7	The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 may be machined, cast, molded or fabricated from metal or from a reinforced polymer, the material being chosen for the service environment. The hinge 16 may be a pin hinge, a pair of interleaved knuckles on a common pin, or a flexible hinge section integral with the frame, provided that it holds the frame halves in register when they are closed. Closure of the frame halves in register is relied upon by the cam drive described below, so the hinge 16 and the releasable latch 18 are arranged to bring the two frame halves to a repeatable closed position rather than merely to hold them near one another.
8	
9	A plurality of jaw carriages 22 is distributed circumferentially about the closed frame. In the form shown in FIG. 1 the plurality of jaw carriages 22 consists of three jaw carriages 22 distributed about the closed frame. Three carriages define a stable seat on a round pipe without over constraining it. The synchronizing relationship described below is not limited to that number, and a clamp having more than three jaw carriages 22 is built in the same way, each additional jaw carriage 22 being coupled to the cam ring by its own follower and its own oblique slot as described below.
10	
11	The frame carries a mounting boss 66, which stands radially outside the cam drive described below. The mounting boss 66 supports a sensor, a tool or a conduit on the split pipe clamp 10 and may be a threaded pad, a dovetail, a flange with fastener holes, or any other fitting suitable for the item to be carried. The mounting boss 66 does not participate in advancing or synchronizing the jaw carriages 22. A load applied to the mounting boss 66 is therefore reacted through the frame and into the jaw pads, and is not carried by the cam drive, so a moment applied by a carried instrument does not disturb the setting of the jaws.
12	
13	Jaw carriages and jaw pads
14	
15	Referring to FIG. 2, each jaw carriage 22 is slidable in a respective radial guide 24 of the frame. The radial guide 24 may be a rectangular slideway, a pair of parallel rails, or a bore that receives a cylindrical shank of the jaw carriage 22, and it constrains the jaw carriage 22 to travel along a radial path toward and away from the central axis of the closed frame. In the illustrated form two of the radial guides 24 are formed in one of the frame halves and a remaining one of the radial guides 24 is formed in the other frame half, so that each frame half carries at least one jaw carriage 22 and each frame half is loaded by the clamping action.
16	
17	Each jaw carriage 22 carries a jaw pad 26 that is mounted on the jaw carriage 22 for pivoting movement about a pad axis and that presents a concave bearing surface toward the central axis of the closed frame. Because the jaw pad 26 pivots relative to the jaw carriage 22, the concave bearing surface aligns itself with the surface of the pipe 20 that it meets, and bears on the pipe over an area rather than along an edge. The split pipe clamp 10 therefore grips pipes over a range of diameters and does not require a tool specific pipe diameter. The pad axis is parallel to the axis of the pipe 20 in the illustrated form, and the jaw pad 26 may be faced with an elastomer, with a soft metal, or with a friction material where the pipe surface is to be protected.
18	
19	A carriage spring 42 biases each jaw carriage 22 outward, away from the central axis of the closed frame. The carriage spring 42 may be a compression spring seated in the radial guide 24, a tension spring acting between the jaw carriage 22 and the frame, or a leaf element. When the releasable latch 18 is released, the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22 and lift the jaw pads 26 clear of the pipe 20, so that the frame halves can be swung apart without the jaw pads 26 dragging on the pipe.
20	
21	The segmented cam ring
22	
23	A cam ring 30 is retained in an annular guide 36 of the frame, as shown in FIG. 2. The annular guide 36 is an annular channel of the frame, concentric with the central axis of the closed frame, that locates the cam ring 30 radially and axially while allowing it to rotate through a limited stroke about that axis. Because the annular guide 36 continues around both frame halves, the reaction to the clamping load is taken by the frame around the whole arc rather than across the split line between the frame halves.
24	
25	The mounting boss 66 stands on the frame radially outside the annular guide 36, clear of the cam ring 30 and of the jaw carriages 22.
26	
27	The cam ring 30 is segmented. Referring to FIG. 3, the cam ring 30 comprises a first cam-ring segment 32 and a second cam-ring segment 34. The first cam-ring segment 32 is carried by the first frame half 12 and the second cam-ring segment 34 is carried by the second frame half 14, each segment being retained by the frame half that carries it. Each segment accordingly stays with its own frame half when the frame is opened, and the frame halves can be swung fully apart without dismantling the drive.
28	
29	The first cam-ring segment 32 has a hinge-end drive face 44 and a latch-end drive face 48. The second cam-ring segment 34 has a hinge-end drive face 46 and a latch-end drive face 50. The hinge-end drive face 44 and the hinge-end drive face 46 are complementary to one another, and the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 are complementary to one another. Closing the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 at the hinge end and brings the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50 at the latch end, and thereby couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 so that they rotate together as one cam ring 30 about the central axis of the closed frame.
30	
31	The complementary drive faces may be plain abutment faces lying in radial planes, faces inclined so that one segment end laps the other, or a tongue on one segment received in a recess of the other. What matters is that in the closed frame each pair of faces transmits circumferential drive from one segment to the other in the direction of the clamping stroke, and that the faces separate freely when the frame halves are swung apart. The coupling is made by the closing motion of the frame halves themselves, so no fastener, key or separate coupling action is required of the operator, and there is no state in which the frame is closed but the drive is not yet made up.
32

# FIG. 1

View: front elevation of the clamp closed around a pipe, along the pipe axis. Patent line drawing, black line work on white, no shading or color. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

Geometry to draw:

- A pipe drawn as one plain circle at the center of the drawing area, occupying roughly the middle third of its width. The interior of the circle is empty.
- Around that circle, an annular frame body drawn as an outer boundary and an inner boundary, concentric with the pipe circle and spaced outward from it, so a band of frame material surrounds the pipe. It is divided into two substantially semicircular halves by two radial breaks, one at the left and one at the right, the upper half and the lower half being drawn as separate solids meeting at those breaks.
- At the left break, a hinge drawn as a small circle straddling the two halves, with a short pair of straight lines joining it to each half, so the halves are visibly pivoted together there.
- At the right break, a latch drawn as a compact rectangular body attached across the two halves and overlapping both, with a straight lever arm extending outward and downward to the right.
- Three carriage blocks at roughly equal angular intervals, one at the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, none of them at either break. Each is a small rectangle whose long dimension is radial, passing through the inner boundary of the annular frame body and stopping short of the pipe circle.
- Between the inner end of each carriage block and the pipe circle, a small block whose inner edge is a concave arc meeting the pipe circle, so that this small block, and not the carriage block, contacts the pipe.
- A mounting boss drawn as a small rectangular pad on the outer boundary of the annular frame body at the upper right, projecting radially outward and joined to it.

The hinge, the latch, the small blocks at the inner ends of the carriage blocks, and the mounting boss are shown schematically.

Reference numerals appearing on this sheet: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 66.

Numeral placement targets:

- 10: the outer boundary line at the lower left, identifying the assembly as a whole.
- 12: well inside the upper half of the annular frame body.

- 18: well inside the rectangular latch body at the right break.
- 20: the interior of the pipe circle.

# FIG. 2

View: front interior view of the closed clamp along the pipe axis. Patent line drawing, black on white, no shading or color. Near side frame material is omitted so the interior is open to view, a depiction convention. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

Geometry to draw:

- An annular body drawn as concentric outer and inner boundary circles centered in the drawing area. The space between them is open, without hatching; the region inside the inner circle is empty and no pipe is drawn.
- Within that space, a narrow band of two concentric arcs set toward the outer boundary. This band is the cam ring, divided at two diametrically opposite locations, left and right, each division drawn as a short line across the band.
- Outboard of the band, a channel outline of two further concentric arcs between the band and the outer circle, so the band sits in that channel, drawn in the arc stretches between the slideways.
- Three slideways through the annular body at roughly equal angular intervals, one at the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, none at either division. Each is a pair of parallel straight lines running radially between the boundary circles.
- In each slideway a carriage drawn as a radially long rectangle, narrower than the slideway so the guide lines stay visible on both sides. Each carriage stops short of the inner circle and reaches the band at its outer end.
- On the inner end of each carriage a pad drawn as a small block whose inner edge is a concave arc curving away from the center of the view, joined to the carriage at a small circle.
- At the outer end of each carriage a small circle representing a follower, lying on the band, and around it a slot drawn as an elongated closed outline through the band, inclined so its long direction is neither purely radial nor purely along the band. The slots share one rotational sense.
- In the outer stretch of each slideway, between the carriage and the outer circle, a spring drawn as a short zigzag line.

The cam ring, followers and springs are shown schematically.

Reference numerals appearing on this sheet: 22, 24, 26, 30, 36, 38, 40, 42.

- 38: the slot outline at the lower left, clear of the follower circle in it.
